title: Torus centralizers preserve reductivity
statement: Let $F$ be an algebraically closed field [def-weil-field, def-weil-algebraic-closure]. All groups are affine group schemes [def-sc-group-scheme] of finite type [def-weil-finite-type-morphism], and subgroups are closed subgroup schemes [def-sc-group-scheme-subgroup]. Use reductivity, maximal tori, and scheme-theoretic centralizer points as in [def-sfb-reductive-torus-centralizer-terminology]. A torus is a group isomorphic to $\mathbf G_m^r$ for an integer $r\geq0$, where $\mathbf G_m(A)=A^\times$ [def-sc-gm-ga]. Let $G$ be reductive and let $S\subseteq G$ be any torus, not necessarily maximal. Then the centralizer functor $C_G(S)$ is represented by a reductive closed subgroup scheme of $G$. In particular it is smooth and connected. Smoothness is as in [def-sbc-smooth-morphisms], and connectedness as in [def-weil-connected-scheme].

source.place: Corollary 17.59, printed p.371; its proof uses Corollary 17.57 (unipotent radical of a torus centralizer), Theorem 17.38, and Corollary 13.9.

proof.text: Choose a torus $T\subseteq G$ containing $S$ of greatest dimension. Such a choice exists: $S$ is one candidate, tori are smooth and connected by [lem-sfb-multiplicative-type-largest-subtorus], and their dimensions are nonnegative integers bounded by $\dim G$ by [lem-sfb-solvable-normal-subgroup-products]. The same node says a proper inclusion of smooth connected groups strictly increases dimension. Thus no larger torus contains $T$, so $T$ is maximal.

source.place: Corollary 17.57, proof: choose a maximal torus containing S; greatest-dimension argument as in Proposition 6.42, printed p.134.

proof.text: By [lem-sfb-torus-centralizer-smooth-connected], the functor $C_G(S)$ is represented by a smooth connected closed subgroup $C\subseteq G$. Its all-algebras centralizer condition is exactly the condition in the item. In particular $C$ is an affine finite-type group to which the cited structure theorems apply. It remains to exclude nontrivial smooth connected normal unipotent subgroups of $C$.

source.place: Corollary 17.59, proof, printed p.371; Corollary 13.10 and Theorem 17.38.

proof.text: Let $U\subseteq C$ be any smooth connected normal unipotent closed subgroup. It is solvable by [lem-sfb-smooth-unipotent-solvable]. Apply [lem-sfb-general-borel-flag-variety] to the smooth connected group $C$, obtaining the nonempty proper finite-type scheme $X=\mathcal B(C)$ with its $C$-action and the stated Borel stabilizers. Restrict this action to $U$. By [lem-sfb-solvable-proper-fixed-point] there is $x=b_D\in X(F)$ fixed scheme-theoretically by $U$, where $D$ is a Borel of $C$.

source.place: Corollary 17.57, proof, containment in Borel subgroups; expanded using Theorems 17.3 and 17.9 and Proposition 14.21.

proof.text: For any Borel $D\subseteq C$, write $b_D=c\cdot x$ with $c\in C(F)$ using the transitivity in [lem-sfb-general-borel-flag-variety]. For every commutative $F$-algebra $A$ and $u\in U(A)$, normality gives $c_A^{-1}uc_A\in U(A)$. Therefore $u\cdot(b_D)_A=c_A\cdot((c_A^{-1}uc_A)\cdot x_A)=c_A\cdot x_A=(b_D)_A$. The same node identifies the scheme-theoretic stabilizer of $b_D$ with $D$, so $U\subseteq D$ on every test algebra. This uses the fixed point from step 3 and proves the needed containment without passing from rational points to subgroup schemes.

source.place: Corollary 17.57, proof: the unipotent radical lies in each Borel; elementary normality calculation with Theorem 17.9.

proof.text: For each Borel subgroup $B\subseteq G$ containing $T$, we also have $S\subseteq B$. By [lem-sfb-torus-centralizer-borel-intersection], $D_B=C\cap B$ is a Borel subgroup of $C$. Step 4 gives $U\subseteq D_B\subseteq B$ as closed subgroup functors. Hence $U\to G$ factors through the scheme-theoretic intersection $I=\bigcap_{B\supseteq T}B$: on affine coordinate rings the sum of the ideals of the $B$ maps to zero.

source.place: Corollary 17.57, proof, printed p.371; Theorem 17.46, printed pp.365--366.

proof.text: The scheme $U$ is reduced, since it is smooth over a field by [sbc-lem-smooth-geometrically-reduced]. By [lem-weil-pbc-reduced-source-factors-through-closed-subscheme], $U\to I$ factors through $I_{\mathrm{red}}$. Its image is connected and contains the identity, so it is contained in the identity component; the same reduced-source factorization statement gives a factorization through $(I_{\mathrm{red}})^\circ$. By [lem-sfb-chevalley-borel-intersection], this closed subgroup equals $R_u(G)\cdot T$. Here $R_u(G)$ is the largest smooth connected normal unipotent subgroup of $G$ in that node. Reductivity of $G$ makes this subgroup trivial by [def-sfb-reductive-torus-centralizer-terminology]. Thus $(I_{\mathrm{red}})^\circ=T$, and the original inclusion $U\to G$ factors through $T\to G$.

source.place: Corollary 17.57, reverse inclusion, and Theorem 17.56, first equality, printed p.371; its reduced identity-component interpretation.

proof.text: The homomorphism $U\to T$ is trivial by [lem-sfb-unipotent-to-multiplicative-trivial], since $U$ is smooth unipotent in its equivalent geometric-matrix sense and $T\simeq\mathbf G_m^r$ is of multiplicative type. Its composite $U\to G$ is the original closed subgroup inclusion and is therefore a monomorphism. A trivial monomorphism of group functors has only the identity as an $A$-point for every $A$, so $U$ is the trivial group scheme. As $U$ was arbitrary, $C$ is reductive by [def-sfb-reductive-torus-centralizer-terminology]; the base field is already algebraically closed. Together with step 2 this proves all clauses.

source.place: Corollary 17.57, final unipotent subgroup argument, and Corollary 17.59, printed p.371; Corollary 14.18 (unipotent to multiplicative type).

proof_origin.place: Corollary 17.59, proof via the reverse inclusion of Corollary 17.57 and Theorem 17.56, printed p.371. The containment in Borels is expanded by Theorems 17.3 and 17.9.

It adds no new nodes and splits the item into 7 steps over 12 existing nodes; the inherited statement is unchanged apart from listing def-weil-field and def-weil-algebraic-closure in stmt_deps. Source checked in the PDF: Milne iAG2017 Cor 17.59 (p.371) and the reverse inclusion of Cor 17.57, Thm 17.46 (p.365) and Thm 17.56 (Chevalley). Step 1: by lem-sfb-multiplicative-type-largest-subtorus and the dimension clauses of lem-sfb-solvable-normal-subgroup-products, a torus T above S of greatest dimension is maximal in the sense the Chevalley node uses. Step 2: the centralizer functor of torus-centralizer-smooth-connected is the same as the C_i of the terminology node. Step 3: smooth-unipotent-solvable (series form) matches the derived-series form used by the flag and fixed-point nodes, which def-sfb-solvable-group-structure records as the same notion; the flag variety of C plus the fixed-point lemma give a U-fixed point b_D. Step 4: transitivity, the all-algebras stabilizer clause and A-point normality from def-sc-group-scheme-subgroup put U in every Borel of C on all test algebras. Step 5: torus-centralizer-borel-intersection applies because S is in T, which is in B. Step 6: U is reduced, so it factors through (I_red)°; this equals R_u(G)T, and R_u(G)=1 by reductivity, so U lies in T. Step 7: the unipotent-to-multiplicative node's notion matches for smooth U, so U→T is trivial and U=1 because the inclusion is a monomorphism. Edge cases checked: trivial S, central S, G a torus, trivial G, mu_p/alpha_p in characteristic p; the proof never deduces scheme equality from F-points. No cycle (the deps' closure excludes the item and its citer). No duplicate found by rg -L. sbc smooth-geometrically-reduced and pbc reduced-source factorization are generic tool_uses, which I accept.
